description: Fig. 11 is a composite schematic (no axes, no scale bars, no numeric labels) comparing impact-fracture crack propagation in two low-alloy ultrahigh-strength steels, labelled "0Al" (top row) and "1.3Al" (bottom row) on pale-blue tabs at the far left. Each row contains a left hexagonal cell showing the pre-stress substructure and a right hexagonal cell showing the post-"High stress" state; a broad arrow labelled "High stress" sits between the two columns. In the 0Al left cell, sparsely distributed blue ε-carbide rectangles, dashed lines and a few dislocations are drawn; the 1.3Al left cell is densely filled with red NiAl spheres together with ε-carbide and dislocations. After high stress the 0Al cell shows a relatively direct zigzag crack with a dense tangled network of dislocations near the fracture path and no voids, whereas the 1.3Al cell shows a strongly deflected, stair-step crack path with black-arrowheaded secondary cracks and yellow voids arrowed along it. A separate detail at the right shows red NiAl spheres and elongated blue ε-carbide ovals interacting with squiggly dislocation lines. The bottom legend defines: red sphere = NiAl, blue dash = ε-carbide, squiggly line = dislocation, black arrowhead = secondary crack, yellow dot = void.

subfigures.description: Hexagonal cell for the '0Al' steel before loading: sparsely distributed blue ε-carbide dashes, dashed short lines and a few dislocation squiggles in an otherwise empty matrix; no red NiAl spheres are drawn.

Hexagonal cell for '0Al' after the 'High stress' arrow: a zigzag crack running across the cell edge, the upper region filled with a dense tangled network of dislocation lines, and no voids or secondary cracks marked.

Hexagonal cell for the '1.3Al' steel before loading: high density of red NiAl spheres plus blue ε-carbide dashes and dislocation lines distributed throughout the cell, clearly denser in obstacles than the 0Al cell.

Hexagonal cell for '1.3Al' after 'High stress': strongly stair-stepped, tortuous crack path across the cell, black arrowhead symbols marking secondary cracks branching from the main path, and yellow voids arrowed along the crack, all embedded in a dense network of dislocation squiggles, NiAl spheres and ε-carbide.

Schematic detail to the right of the lower cell showing individual squiggly dislocation lines interacting with red NiAl spheres (clusters sitting on/near the lines) and with a cluster of elongated blue ε-carbide ovals bridged by a dislocation.
Legend row defining symbols: red sphere = NiAl, blue dash = ε-carbide, squiggly line = dislocation, black arrowhead = secondary crack, yellow dot = void.

observations.observation: The figure contains no axes, no scale bars and no printed numeric values; it is a purely qualitative schematic of impact-fracture crack propagation.
Two alloy conditions are labelled on the left-hand blue tabs: '0Al' (upper row) and '1.3Al' (lower row).
A broad arrow labelled 'High stress' connects the left (pre-stress) column of hexagonal cells to the right (post-stress) column.

The pre-stress 1.3Al cell contains a markedly higher density of obstacles (red NiAl spheres plus blue ε-carbide dashes) than the pre-stress 0Al cell, which shows only ε-carbide dashes and a few dislocations.
After high stress, the 0Al cell shows a comparatively direct zigzag crack with a dense tangled dislocation network adjacent to the path, and no secondary cracks or voids are drawn.
After high stress, the 1.3Al cell shows a strongly deflected, stair-step crack path with black arrowhead symbols marking secondary cracks and yellow dots marking voids along the path.
The legend at the bottom defines: red sphere = NiAl, blue dash = ε-carbide, squiggly line = dislocation, black arrowhead = secondary crack, yellow dot = void.
The isolated detail at the right shows dislocations drawn as squiggly lines interacting with NiAl spheres and with elongated ε-carbide ovals that dislocations appear to bypass.
The caption states the figure is a schematic illustration of crack propagation behaviour during impact fracture.

The citing text states that in the 1.3Al steel ε-carbides promote dislocation cell formation through bypassing while closely spaced NiAl clusters are directly sheared, giving a more uniform spatial distribution of dislocations.

The citing text states that at high stress the crack path is deflected by NiAl-induced perturbations and disrupted by secondary cracks initiated via void coalescence, increasing crack tortuosity and retarding propagation.
The citing text states that the refined dislocation network suppresses localized strain accumulation and raises the energy barrier for crack initiation, resulting in greater energy absorption.
